newsitem.title: USA: Quaker chairman says company stronger post-Snapple.
newsitem.headline: Quaker chairman says company stronger post-Snapple.

text.p: Quaker Oats Co., after weathering the Snapple storm for two years, is sailing smoothly, Chairman William Smithburg says.
"People are recognizing that, gosh, the 90 percent of the company that wasn't Snapple is doing well -- in fact, extremely well," Smithburg, who plans to retire this year, said late Wednesday.
With its $1.5 billion Gatorade sports drink and its 100-year-old Quaker brand of cereals, oatmeal and rice cakes, the company's portfolio is the strongest it has ever been, he added.

"In virtually every case we're outperforming the competition. We're showing excellent margins, good growth, good market share, good improvement," Smithburg said, as he took sips from a bottle of lemon-lime-flavored Gatorade.

Chicago-based Quaker, with about $5.0 billion in annual sales, posted stronger-than-expected earnings in the second quarter, helping to boost the stock to a new high of $52 a share this week. Quaker stock rose 25 cents to $50.875 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
"I think Bill Smithburg has been through a very difficult period," Merrill Lynch analyst Eric Katzman said. "He feels he has turned around the ship and has it headed in the right direction."
But Snapple -- which Quaker Oats bought in a $1.8 billion transaction in late 1994 and sold in a deal worth a total of $550 million in May -- took its toll on Quaker.
The fruit-flavored beverage and iced tea business never posted a profit for Quaker except, oddly, in the last few weeks that Quaker owned the business that was sold to Triarc Cos. Inc.
There has been speculation that Smithburg, 58, is retiring as a direct result of the failed Snapple acquisition.
Smithburg would not comment on his decision to retire, except to say the timing is right for Quaker and for him.
"If you turn the clock back to last fall, we were getting bad press all focused on Snapple ... and it was tough. You don't move on at a time like that," Smithburg said. "You resolve the issue."
He did not say when Quaker would name his successor other than to reiterate that the process, which began in April, was one of "months, not weeks."
But it appears Smithburg expects to step down by year-end. "I'm a skier, and I plan to do a lot of skiing this year."

Going forward, one of Quaker's growth areas is likely to be its Gatorade sports drink -- an acquisition that Smithburg counts as one of the highlights of his Quaker career -- which holds about 83 percent of the domestic market.
To increase sales further, Smithburg said Gatorade must broaden the category, competing with a host of beverages from soft drinks to water.
When Quaker bought Gatorade in 1983 as part of its $238 million acquisition of Stokely-Van Camp, the beverage had only $90 million in annual sales.
"That, again, is part of taking risk. No market research is going to guarantee you that it's going to work out," Smithburg said of the Gatorade acquisition.
Snapple, which Quaker had hoped to pair with Gatorade, clearly did not work out.

"You never bat 100 percent, and we obviously did not succeed with that acquisition. The synergies with Gatorade did not materialize," Smithburg said. "What you have to do is, you cut your losses and move out."
